metadata.assigned_reading: Buterin, Vitalik. The Meaning of Decentralization.
metadata.grounding_note: Questions emphasize contingent blockchain futures, adoption friction, institutional and crypto-native trajectories, AI and quantum risks, decentralization dimensions, and trust relocation while avoiding dates, organization-name recall, and standalone trivia.

lectures.title: Future Trajectories and Synthesis - lesson slides
Future Trajectories and Synthesis - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A policy analyst predicts that blockchains will either become the universal backbone of finance or disappear as failed technology. Which response best reflects the lesson's framing?
questions.correct_answer: Multiple futures can coexist because adoption depends on sector-specific incentives, constraints, geography, regulation, and user trust.
incorrect_answers: A single universal settlement layer must emerge because every sector faces identical incentives, rules, geography, and user trust requirements.
Blockchains must disappear because regulators, users, institutions, and developers will reject every distributed ledger design globally soon.
Cryptographic progress alone will determine the future because geography, regulation, incentives, user trust, and sector needs no longer matter.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames blockchain's future as contingent and path-dependent, with infrastructure-scale adoption, crypto-native persistence, and fragmentation able to appear in different domains at the same time.

provenance.source_anchor: Futures As A Spectrum, Not A Prediction

questions.question_stem: A central bank, major banks, and regulated payment firms adopt tokenized settlement rails for faster cross-border transfers. What is the main tradeoff the lesson asks students to notice?
questions.correct_answer: Institutional settlement may preserve programmability and faster reconciliation while weakening permissionless autonomy and decentralization ideals.
incorrect_answers: Institutional settlement may remove regulation and fees while guaranteeing personal custody, censorship resistance, and full financial privacy.
Institutional settlement may create fully permissionless autonomy while preserving every central bank control and compliance checkpoint.
Institutional settlement may replace sovereign money entirely while eliminating intermediaries, compliance checks, and custody risks too.
questions.explanation: The global settlement-layer trajectory is plausible partly because institutions value programmability and settlement efficiency, but this pathway can reintroduce gatekeepers, compliance control, and centralized oversight.

questions.question_stem: A blockchain ecosystem remains important for DeFi, tokenized communities, NFTs, and on-chain governance, but most consumers never use it for ordinary payments. Which future trajectory does this best illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: A specialized crypto-native ecosystem that persists by creating bounded value without replacing mainstream infrastructure.
incorrect_answers: A complete technical failure in which core protocols cannot process transactions, govern assets, or support communities.
A global settlement infrastructure that expands by enforcing rigid rules without changing traditional payment systems.
A fragmented decline trajectory that loses public trust while retaining no active localized communities or markets.
questions.explanation: The specialized ecosystem trajectory treats durable but bounded crypto-native value as a plausible outcome. Blockchain can matter in specific markets and communities without becoming universal infrastructure.

questions.question_stem: A technically working blockchain platform struggles because users find key management risky, regulators restrict access, fees spike under load, and trusted non-blockchain systems already solve the main business problem. What lesson concept best explains this outcome?
questions.correct_answer: Adoption is limited by accumulated friction across technology, institutions, economics, usability, and legitimacy.
incorrect_answers: Adoption is guaranteed automatically by full legitimacy across sovereign states, central banks, and global markets worldwide.
Adoption is governed solely by consensus mechanics across network latency, computational limits, and throughput metrics.
Adoption is driven entirely by cryptographic security across signing schemes, hash functions, and secret keys alone.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that blockchain adoption is rarely blocked by a single flaw. Technical limits, legal constraints, user experience, trust, competition, and economic incentives interact.

provenance.source_anchor: Adoption Is Limited By Accumulated Friction

questions.question_stem: A team improves transaction throughput by moving most activity to a scaling layer, but users must now accept added complexity and new trust assumptions. What is the best interpretation?
questions.correct_answer: The scaling layer may improve capacity while relocating complexity and trust assumptions rather than eliminating the scalability tradeoff.
incorrect_answers: The scaling layer may bypass base-layer rules while standardizing wallets and interfaces, fully solving the blockchain trilemma for every user.
The scaling layer may maximize throughput while eliminating latency and fees without introducing new assumptions or operational complexity.
The scaling layer may automate transaction signing while removing consensus rules, data availability limits, and all user custody risks entirely.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats scalability improvements as real but not free. Higher throughput can come with added complexity, latency, governance dependencies, or new assumptions about who must be trusted.

questions.question_stem: A DAO's voting rules execute exactly as coded, but wealthy early insiders repeatedly pass proposals that benefit themselves and weaken long-term project stability. What does this show?
questions.correct_answer: Protocol correctness does not by itself solve governance, incentive alignment, or concentration of power.
incorrect_answers: Protocol correctness ensures that incentives align automatically and token-voting power stays decentralized.
On-chain voting ensures all decisions maximize long-term project stability regardless of insider wealth.
Wealthy token holders can bypass execution rules to alter ledger state without governance calls.
questions.explanation: The lesson highlights human and economic constraints: formal rules can execute correctly while incentives, voting concentration, insider power, or short-term gain undermine the system.

questions.question_stem: A proof-of-work blockchain keeps running securely, but energy controversy, price volatility, and compliance concerns make institutions reluctant to build on it. Which constraint category is most central here?
questions.correct_answer: External legitimacy constraints can limit adoption even when the protocol continues to function.
incorrect_answers: Internal scalability limits can block transactions even when validator networks remain decentralized.
Private key custody risks can deter institutions even when signature algorithms remain secure.
Consensus liveness failures can halt blocks even as public legitimacy and compliance improve.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats regulation, energy and resource concerns, volatility, geopolitical pressure, and public legitimacy as forces that shape adoption independently of narrow protocol liveness.

questions.question_stem: A security team uses AI to scan smart contracts and monitor fraud patterns, while attackers use similar tools to discover exploitable bugs and scale automated large-scale attacks. What is the lesson's main point about AI and blockchain?
questions.correct_answer: AI can amplify both defensive operations and offensive risks, compressing the time between discovery and irreversible on-chain consequences.
incorrect_answers: AI can automate smart contract auditing so completely that manual monitoring, incident response, and off-chain coordination become unnecessary.
AI can bypass cryptographic signatures and consensus protocols, reducing the cost of Sybil attacks and double-spending transactions.
AI can eliminate economic volatility and validator censorship, securing networks against transaction spam and malicious protocol forks.
questions.explanation: The lesson rejects generic convergence hype. It asks students to distinguish concrete opportunities such as auditing and monitoring from risks such as faster exploit discovery, automated large-scale attacks, exploit scanning, and governance manipulation.

provenance.source_anchor: AI And Blockchain Create Interaction Effects

questions.question_stem: A news organization records content credentials and edit history on a blockchain-backed provenance system. Which claim should students reject?
questions.correct_answer: The record proves the content is true because blockchain provenance can verify real-world accuracy by itself.
incorrect_answers: The record can improve auditability when provenance chains and media edit history remain continually maintained.
The record may help preserve origin and edits if capture, signing, and custody processes remain trustworthy.
The record can make later tampering easier to detect without removing cryptographic trust questions.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats provenance as a partial response to synthetic media and authenticity problems. It can support origin and change tracking, but it cannot by itself prove truth, trustworthy capture, or correct interpretation.

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson describe quantum risk as a governance and migration problem, not just a cryptography problem?
questions.correct_answer: Even if post-quantum tools exist, wallets, clients, exchanges, standards, ownership proofs, and users must coordinate a staged transition before assumptions fail.
incorrect_answers: Even if quantum computers arrive, miners, validators, developers, node operators, and institutions must execute a rapid hard fork before every network collapses.
Even if common algorithms break, signature schemes, block hashes, consensus parameters, and local key systems must update automatically before attackers react.
Even if cryptographic patches exist, user private keys, wallet software, block headers, public networks, and protocols must deploy instantly before keys fail.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes assumption failure under uncertainty. Moving to post-quantum or hybrid systems requires broad coordination across infrastructure, users, custody, standards, and governance.

provenance.source_anchor: Quantum Risk As Assumption Failure And Migration Challenge

questions.question_stem: A blockchain runs on thousands of machines, is governed by many independent actors, and maintains one agreed ledger state. Using Buterin's reading, how should this be described?
questions.correct_answer: It aspires to architectural and political decentralization while remaining logically centralized around a shared state.
incorrect_answers: It features architectural and political centralization while staying logically decentralized across many hardware systems.
It exhibits architectural decentralization but political centralization under one actor and many local states.
It limits architectural and political decentralization while keeping logical centralization inside local databases.
questions.explanation: The reading separates decentralization into architectural, political, and logical axes. Blockchains can distribute machines and control while still behaving like one shared computer with a common state.

provenance.assigned_reading: Buterin, Vitalik. The Meaning of Decentralization.

questions.question_stem: A network advertises 20,000 nodes, but nearly all run the same client software maintained by one small team and many validators keep stake through one exchange. What would Buterin's framework emphasize?
questions.correct_answer: The high node count may mask common-mode failures and political concentration through shared software, developers, and custody.
incorrect_answers: The high node count may prove absolute security and architectural independence through shared systems, clients, and validator sets.
The high node count may guarantee fault tolerance and collusion resistance through shared algorithms, custody, and developers.
The high node count may block external coercion and logical centralization through several clients, protocols, and servers.
questions.explanation: The reading warns that redundancy helps only when components fail independently. Shared clients, concentrated developers, geographic or hardware dependence, and exchange-held stake can create correlated failure or control.

questions.question_stem: A blockchain community can coordinate quickly to patch a serious bug, but the same miners, validators, or developers could also coordinate to censor users or change rules for private gain. Which reading concept best captures this tension?
questions.correct_answer: The governance paradox: blockchains need beneficial coordination while resisting harmful collusion by powerful subgroups.
incorrect_answers: Logical decentralization: databases need total partition survival while keeping single state agreement by independent nodes.
Fault tolerance: operators need identical node replication while eliminating correlated failures by diverse developers.
Attack resistance: validator networks need transaction fees while resisting government coercion by sovereign nations.
questions.explanation: Buterin distinguishes coordination needed for upgrades and maintenance from collusion that exploits less coordinated users. The design challenge is not eliminating coordination but shaping when it is possible and accountable.
